title: Chubb's Third-Quarter Profit Rises to $2.84 Billion as Catastrophe Losses More Than Double to $705 Million and Investment Income Climbs 8.6%
summary: Chubb reported third-quarter 2026 net income of $2.84 billion ($7.30 per share) and a P&C combined ratio of 84.1%, up from 81.8%, as catastrophe losses rose to $705 million from $285 million and favourable reserve development reached $511 million.
description:
Chubb Limited, one of the world's largest property and casualty insurers, reported third-quarter 2026 results on October 20, 2026. The company said net income for the quarter was $2.84 billion, or $7.30 per share, an increase of 4.4% in the per-share figure. Core operating income, which strips out items such as realised investment gains and losses, was $2.98 billion, or $7.66 per share. Chubb's chairman and chief executive, Evan Greenberg, said the company had "a really strong quarter with strong contributions from all of our businesses."

Premium growth was modest. Consolidated net premiums written, the premiums Chubb keeps after reinsurance, were $15.1 billion, up 1.9% from a year earlier. Property and casualty premiums were $13.18 billion, also up 1.9%. The release as summarised for this article does not break growth down by region or division, so it is not possible to say from these figures alone which businesses grew fastest. Greenberg did add a forward-looking comment: "I fully expect North America commercial growth to improve in future quarters." That wording implies commercial growth in North America was weaker than the company would like in the quarter, consistent with the softer commercial pricing reported by brokers such as Marsh.

The most important measure of underwriting performance, the P&C combined ratio, was 84.1%. The combined ratio compares claims and operating costs with premiums, so anything below 100% means an underwriting profit. A year earlier, Chubb's ratio was 81.8%, a record. The deterioration of 2.3 percentage points has an obvious cause: catastrophe losses. Pre-tax catastrophe losses were $705 million in the third quarter of 2026 compared with $285 million in the same quarter of 2025. That is an increase of $420 million, or about 147%. The press release summary does not say which events drove the losses, and it would be wrong to attribute them to a specific storm without that information.

Offsetting some of the losses, Chubb released more reserves than a year earlier. Favourable prior-period development, which occurs when claims from earlier years turn out cheaper than the company had set aside, was $511 million pre-tax compared with $361 million in the prior-year quarter. Insurers watch this item closely because large releases can flatter current results. Even without it, an 84.1% combined ratio would still indicate healthy underwriting, though the exact underlying ratio is not given in the material reviewed.

Investment income continued to grow. Pre-tax net investment income was $1.79 billion, up 8.6%. Adjusted net investment income, which Chubb uses to include certain items on a tax-equivalent basis, was $1.89 billion, up 6.3%. Higher yields on bonds bought in recent years, together with a growing portfolio, are the likely drivers, though the release summary does not set out the reasons. For a company with Chubb's balance sheet, investment income is a second engine of profit alongside underwriting, and it has become more important as interest rates rose after 2022.

How does this fit with the wider market? Marsh's index shows global commercial insurance rates falling about 6% in the second quarter of 2026 and property rates falling 12%, while casualty rates in the United States were still rising 7%. Reinsurance prices are expected to fall again at the January 2027 renewals. Against that background, Chubb is growing premiums by under 2% and still earning an underwriting margin that is the envy of most of the industry. That combination suggests that insurers are still profitable despite falling prices, because claims costs and catastrophes have so far been manageable. It also indicates why competition for business is intense.

The catastrophe loss number deserves context. A rise from $285 million to $705 million is large in percentage terms, but it is small relative to Chubb's quarterly premium of $15.1 billion: $705 million is about 4.7% of consolidated net premiums written, and about 5.3% of the P&C premium. Insurers of Chubb's size plan for catastrophe losses and price for them, which is why even a much heavier quarter leaves the combined ratio in the 80s. Smaller insurers with concentrated exposures can find the same events far more damaging.

For investors, the key questions raised by the results are whether pricing declines will start to erode margins and whether Greenberg's expected improvement in North American commercial growth materialises. For customers, the picture is of an insurer with ample capital and little pressure to raise prices in commercial lines, but one that, like others, is watching catastrophe costs. For regulators and policymakers, Chubb's profits illustrate that the sector's problems in recent years, particularly in home insurance, are concentrated in specific states and lines rather than being a general failure of industry earnings.

A few cautions are in order. This article is based on the figures in Chubb's earnings release filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on October 20, 2026, and on the quotes attributed to Greenberg in it; it does not include analyst estimates or a comparison with consensus forecasts. Several items normally covered in the full release, such as segment results, book value and share repurchases, were not part of the material reviewed. Readers who want those details should consult the filing. The per-share growth rates cited depend on Chubb's share count, which falls as the company buys back stock, so per-share profit can grow faster than total net income.
source_name: Chubb Limited (Q3 2026 earnings release, Form 8-K, October 20, 2026)
image_alt: Financial statements and calculator representing insurer quarterly earnings (illustrative)
key_points: Chubb reported Q3 2026 net income of $2.84 billion, or $7.30 per share (up 4.4%), and core operating income of $2.98 billion, or $7.66 per share.
Consolidated net premiums written were $15.1 billion, up 1.9%, with property and casualty premiums of $13.18 billion, also up 1.9%.
The P&C combined ratio was 84.1% against 81.8% a year earlier, as pre-tax catastrophe losses rose to $705 million from $285 million.
Favourable prior-period reserve development was $511 million pre-tax, up from $361 million, and pre-tax net investment income rose 8.6% to $1.79 billion.
Chairman and CEO Evan Greenberg said he fully expects North America commercial growth to improve in future quarters.
why_it_matters: Chubb is one of the world's largest property and casualty insurers, so its results show how the industry is coping with storm losses, softer commercial pricing and higher investment returns. A combined ratio in the mid-80s means it still earns a large underwriting profit, which explains why insurers are competing hard on price.

title: Home Insurance Now Costs More Than Property Tax in About Two-Thirds of US Counties, Bloomberg Intelligence Finds
summary: A Bloomberg Intelligence analysis finds average homeowner premiums exceed property-tax bills in about two-thirds of US counties, with county-level premiums up 45% in a decade after inflation and the gap widest in the Southeast, where insurance can cost 2.5 to 4 times the tax levy.
description:
For millions of American homeowners, the annual insurance bill has overtaken the property-tax bill. That is the central finding of an analysis by Bloomberg Intelligence, reported by Eric Roston for Bloomberg and republished by Claims Journal on October 20, 2026. The analysis, whose findings were credited to analyst Andrew John Stevenson, found that average home insurance premiums exceed average property-tax bills in about two-thirds of US counties. It draws on data from the US Census, state insurance regulators, and federal weather and transportation agencies.

The size of the change is significant. Averaged at the county level, homeowner premiums rose 45% over a decade after adjusting for inflation. Among the states, Nebraska recorded the largest increase cited, at 79%. The analysis also looks at the cost of weather risk more widely. When the weather-related share of auto premiums is added to home insurance, combined costs exceed property taxes in 75% of counties. In county-level averages, homeowners pay 14% more for insurance than for property tax, and the gap grows to 30% when the weather-related part of auto insurance is included.

The pattern varies a great deal by region. In Southeastern states, insurance can cost 2.5 to 4 times the property-tax levy. That region combines hurricane exposure with relatively low property taxes, so the insurance bill dominates. In the Midwest and Mountain West, hail and winter weather are pushing rates up, led by Colorado, Utah and Minnesota. Hail is also raising auto premiums across the Great Plains and Upper Midwest. In contrast, the Northeast, the West and major metropolitan areas have high property taxes, so higher premiums represent a smaller share of the tax bill. That does not mean homeowners there are insulated from premium increases; it means the comparison with property tax looks less extreme.

Why are premiums rising? The Bloomberg piece points to rising disaster costs. It cites Climate Central data showing that US disaster losses in 2025 averaged $156 billion over five years, about ten times the inflation-adjusted 1985 figure. When insurers pay more in claims, they raise prices, tighten underwriting or leave some markets. The article adds that deductibles are also rising, leaving homeowners to cover more of the recovery costs themselves.

The analysis links insurance to public finances, too. According to the report, the United States has historically funded about 90% of disaster recovery over the past two decades, but the federal share is shrinking toward roughly an even split with local funding. It gives two examples. Texas received $23 billion in federal funds after Hurricane Harvey in 2017, compared with $4 billion in local spending. After the January 2025 Los Angeles fires, California received $2.6 billion in federal funds and spent $3.5 billion locally. If more of the burden falls on states and localities, then property owners and taxpayers may face higher costs from both directions.

An expert quoted in the article, Alexandra Glickman of Arthur J. Gallagher & Co., said policyholders should be "willing to pay the premium for it", given rising risk. The comment reflects the insurance industry's view that higher prices reflect higher risk, and that insurance is a necessary protection rather than a discretionary cost.

This latest finding should be read alongside other data. AM Best reported this month that US homeowners insurers posted a $16.5 billion underwriting profit in 2025, the first since 2019. Premiums are high, but insurers are now profitable on their homeowners books, which suggests that rate increases have been catching up with past losses. Whether prices fall or flatten in 2026 and 2027 will depend on catastrophe experience and on reinsurance costs, which are expected to decline further at the January renewals.

What can homeowners do? Practical steps include comparing quotes from several insurers or through an independent agent, asking about discounts for protective measures such as impact-resistant roofing, shutters or fire-resistant landscaping, and reviewing deductibles with an eye to how much they could pay out of pocket after a loss. In states with insurers of last resort, such as Florida's Citizens, premiums may be higher or coverage more limited, so it is worth understanding the options. Raising a deductible lowers the premium but increases the risk of an unaffordable bill after a storm.

For buyers, the findings imply that insurance quotes should be obtained early in a home purchase, because the monthly cost can change the amount a lender will approve. For policymakers, the data highlight pressures behind current debates about building codes, land-use restrictions in high-risk areas and how disaster costs are shared between the federal government and the states.

There are limits to the analysis as reported. County-level averages mask variation within counties, and the article does not publish the full dataset or a county-by-county ranking. It compares premiums with property-tax bills as averages, not for individual homes, so a particular household could be in the one-third of counties where tax still exceeds insurance, or could pay far more than the average. The figures also combine data from different sources and time periods. Even so, the direction is clear: in much of the country, insuring a home against weather has become a major housing cost in its own right.
source_name: Claims Journal (reprinting Bloomberg, Oct 20, 2026; analysis by Bloomberg Intelligence)
image_alt: House keys and insurance paperwork representing homeowner costs (illustrative)
key_points: Bloomberg Intelligence finds average home insurance premiums exceed average property-tax bills in about two-thirds of US counties.
Averaged at the county level, homeowner premiums rose 45% over a decade after adjusting for inflation, with Nebraska's 79% the largest state increase cited.
Homeowners pay a county-level average of 14% more for insurance than for property tax, or 30% more when the weather-related share of auto premiums is included.
In Southeastern states, insurance can cost 2.5 to 4 times the property-tax levy, while hail and winter weather push rates up in Colorado, Utah and Minnesota.
Disaster losses averaged $156 billion over five years to 2025, about ten times the inflation-adjusted 1985 figure, and the federal share of recovery funding is shrinking toward roughly half.
why_it_matters: For most homeowners the biggest housing bills are the mortgage, property tax and insurance. Insurance is becoming the larger of the last two almost everywhere, which squeezes household budgets and affects how much home a buyer can afford.

title: US Homeowners Insurers Post a $16.5 Billion Underwriting Profit in 2025, Their First Since 2019, as Florida Reserve Releases Flatter the Result, AM Best Says
summary: AM Best reports homeowners multiperil insurers earned a $16.5 billion underwriting profit in 2025 after a $1.3 billion loss in 2024, with the combined ratio improving to 84.5 from 90.7, helped by $4.1 billion of favourable reserve development, Florida tort reform and a calm hurricane season.
description:
After years of losses, American home insurers finally made money from underwriting in 2025. According to a report by credit-rating agency AM Best, covered by Insurance Journal on October 19, 2026, homeowners multiperil insurers in the United States posted an underwriting profit of $16.5 billion in 2025. That compares with an underwriting loss of $1.3 billion in 2024 and is the line's first underwriting gain since 2019. Underwriting profit is the money an insurer makes from premiums after paying claims and operating expenses, before investment income.

The history makes the result striking. AM Best notes that seven of the eight years from 2017 to 2024 were underwriting losses for the homeowners line. Wildfires, hurricanes, severe convective storms, inflation in building materials and labour, and litigation all contributed. In response, insurers raised premiums sharply, tightened their underwriting rules and in some states reduced the number of policies they were willing to write. The turnaround in 2025 therefore reflects both those actions and some favourable conditions.

The combined ratio, which measures claims and expenses as a share of premiums, tells the same story. AM Best reports it improved to 84.5 in 2025 from 90.7 in 2024 and 99.5 in 2023. A ratio under 100 means an underwriting profit. The 2023 figure was only just on the profitable side, while 84.5 implies a margin of about 15 cents on each premium dollar before investment income.

Reserve development played a visible part. Favourable loss-reserve development, which occurs when insurers conclude that claims from earlier years will cost less than they had set aside, totalled $4.1 billion in 2025. AM Best says five groups accounted for 47% of that amount: USAA, American Family, Liberty Mutual, Chubb and RenaissanceRe US. Chubb, which reported its own third-quarter results this week, also released reserves in that quarter, according to its earnings release.

Florida is a prominent part of the explanation. AM Best says tort reform in the state reduced property-related lawsuits, which allowed Florida insurers to release reserves they had held for litigation. The agency says this had an "outsized impact on national underwriting results", partly because Florida is the second-largest insurance market in the country. In effect, a change in the legal environment in one state improved a national statistic.

AM Best lists several other drivers. Insurers raised premiums to better match risk. Rate-increase filings slowed in the second half of 2025, a trend that has continued into 2026, which suggests insurers believe their pricing is now adequate in many places. The 2025 hurricane season was relatively calm. And reinsurance prices softened, lowering the cost of protection that insurers buy to cover large losses. Each of these factors could change: a busy hurricane season, a major wildfire or a renewed rise in repair costs would put pressure on results again.

The article, as available for this summary, does not give total premium or loss figures beyond the numbers above, and its table of the top 20 insurers, led by State Farm, Allstate and USAA, appears only as an image. This article therefore cannot report individual company market shares or loss ratios.

How does this connect with what households are paying? A Bloomberg Intelligence analysis, published on October 20, found that average home insurance premiums exceed property-tax bills in about two-thirds of US counties. Both reports can be true at once. Insurers are profitable on homeowners business because they raised prices, and homeowners are paying much more because of those increases. A profitable line does not mean cheaper insurance; it means that insurers are no longer losing money on average, so further large price increases are less likely to be needed, unless losses rise.

There are some points to keep in mind about the profit figure itself. Underwriting profit across an industry is an average, and the experience of individual insurers and states varied widely. Reserve releases of $4.1 billion represent a meaningful share of the $16.5 billion profit, roughly a quarter, and they depend on estimates that can change. The Florida factor is specific to one state's legal changes. And, as AM Best's own list shows, benign weather and softer reinsurance costs are not permanent features.

For consumers, the most useful interpretation is cautious. Slowing rate filings are a good sign for homeowners who have faced rapid increases, but the data do not promise price cuts. Homeowners in states with high catastrophe exposure should still expect rates to track the risk. For policymakers, the Florida experience is a reminder that legal and regulatory reforms can have large effects on insurance markets, though their long-term consequences for policyholders and for access to justice continue to be debated.

For investors and the insurance industry, the numbers indicate a recovery in a line that many insurers had considered unprofitable. The question for 2026 and 2027 is whether the combination of higher premiums, calmer weather and cheaper reinsurance holds. If it does, more insurers may re-enter markets they left; if it does not, the 2025 profit may prove to have been the exception rather than the new normal.
source_name: AM Best, as reported by Insurance Journal (Oct 19, 2026)
image_alt: Residential street after a storm representing homeowners insurance losses (illustrative)
key_points: AM Best says US homeowners multiperil insurers posted a $16.5 billion underwriting profit in 2025, after a $1.3 billion loss in 2024 and the line's first underwriting gain since 2019.
Seven of the eight years from 2017 to 2024 were underwriting losses; the combined ratio improved to 84.5 in 2025 from 90.7 in 2024 and 99.5 in 2023.
Favourable reserve development totalled $4.1 billion in 2025, with USAA, American Family, Liberty Mutual, Chubb and RenaissanceRe US accounting for 47% of it.
Florida tort reform reduced property-related lawsuits and let insurers release reserves, which AM Best says had an outsized impact on national results.
Other drivers were premium increases to match risk, slowing rate filings in the second half of 2025, a relatively calm 2025 hurricane season and softening reinsurance prices.
why_it_matters: Homeowners insurance has been the most troubled personal line for years, with insurers raising prices and leaving states. A return to underwriting profit suggests premiums have caught up with losses, which may slow future rate increases, but the result leaned on reserve releases and a quiet storm season.

title: Google Cloud Outage in London Region Disrupts Revolut, Lloyds and HSBC Services, Putting UK Critical Third-Party Oversight to an Early Test
summary: A 'power event' in Google Cloud's europe-west2 London region caused an hours-long outage on October 20, 2026 that affected Revolut card payments and ATM withdrawals and was reported by Lloyds and HSBC customers; the FCA said it is working with Google and affected firms.
description:
A power problem at a single Google data-centre region disrupted parts of the UK's financial system on Tuesday, October 20, 2026. According to a Reuters report published by Insurance Journal, Google said its UK cloud services were "back up" after an hours-long outage. The company attributed the disruption to a "power event" in its europe-west2 cloud region, which is based in London. The article does not give exact start or end times, so the precise duration is not known from the sources used here.

The financial services impact was visible. Revolut, the digital bank, reported disruption to multiple services, including card payments and ATM withdrawals, and said customers' money and data were unaffected. Lloyds Bank and HSBC appeared in reports on the outage-tracking site Downdetector. Lloyds said it expected services to return to normal soon, and HSBC acknowledged that some customers had trouble accessing its services. ING Germany flagged website and app issues, but said it saw no sign of an external cause or any third-party link, so its problem should not be attributed to Google on the basis of this report.

The disruption extended beyond banking. Downdetector also showed reports involving the property website Rightmove, the parcel firm DPD, NHS England and Royal Mail. Royal Mail said its letter and parcel deliveries were not affected. A Downdetector report indicates that users are having problems; it does not prove the cause or the scale of the problem, so these should be read as signs of possible links, not confirmed impacts.

The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) responded quickly. It said: "We are aware of an incident affecting services provided by Google." It added that it is working with Google and affected firms to assess the impact. The regulator's statement shows how closely the authorities now watch concentration in cloud services.

The timing is notable because of recent regulation. According to the report, in July the UK placed Google Cloud, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services and Oracle under direct oversight as critical third-party providers to the financial sector. Under the regime, which allows HM Treasury to designate providers whose failure could threaten financial stability, regulators can set requirements directly for the technology companies rather than only for the banks that use them. The report also notes that last year EU regulators designated Google Cloud among 19 critical third-party computing providers. The outage therefore arrived only a few months after the UK brought the firms into its supervisory perimeter, and the regulators' handling of this incident will be a first practical test of the arrangement.

What does it mean for insurance? The Reuters article, as carried by Insurance Journal, does not discuss insurance coverage, insured losses or claims. The page is tagged with "business interruption" and "cloud insurance", but gives no details of either. Any analysis of insurance consequences is therefore general and should not be read as a report on actual claims. In general terms, cyber and business interruption policies can cover losses when a firm's operations are interrupted by an outage at a technology supplier, but the cover varies. Some policies include dependent business interruption cover for outages at named or unnamed third-party providers, often with waiting periods of several hours before losses count, and some exclude infrastructure failures such as power or utility problems unless specifically added. Whether any of the affected firms will claim, and whether their policies would respond, is not known.

The wider point concerns concentration risk. When many firms use the same cloud region, a single failure can affect all of them at once, which is the kind of correlated loss that insurers and regulators worry about most. A well-known aggregation concern for cyber insurers is that a cloud outage could trigger claims across many policyholders in a short period. Insurers manage this through policy wording, waiting periods, limits and exclusions for widespread events. Firms that rely on a cloud provider can reduce their own exposure by spreading critical workloads across regions or providers, testing failovers and agreeing recovery plans, although doing so costs money and adds complexity.

For customers, the practical lesson is that payments systems can fail for reasons outside their bank's control. People who rely on a single card or app for essential spending may want a back-up option, such as a second card from a different provider and some cash. Customers who have lost money because of an outage should contact their provider; the Revolut statement says that balances were unaffected.

For regulators, the incident supports the argument that operational resilience, meaning the ability to keep critical services running through disruption, is as important as capital. The FCA's review will show how many firms were affected, how long services were down and whether they stayed within the limits for impact they have set for themselves. The sources used here do not report any findings yet. Further information from Google about the cause of the power event, and from the FCA about its assessment, would help clarify how serious the outage was and what lessons follow.
source_name: Reuters, as published by Insurance Journal (October 20, 2026)
image_alt: Data centre servers representing cloud infrastructure (illustrative)
key_points: Google said its UK cloud services were back up on October 20, 2026 after an hours-long outage that it attributed to a 'power event' in its europe-west2 region, based in London.
Revolut reported disruption to multiple services including card payments and ATM withdrawals, saying customer money and data were unaffected; Lloyds and HSBC appeared in Downdetector reports.
Downdetector also showed reports involving Rightmove, DPD, NHS England and Royal Mail, though Royal Mail said letter and parcel deliveries were not affected.
The FCA said it is aware of an incident affecting services provided by Google and is working with Google and affected firms to assess the impact.
In July the UK placed Google Cloud, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services and Oracle under direct oversight as critical third-party providers to the financial sector.
why_it_matters: Banks, insurers and payment firms increasingly run on a handful of cloud providers, so one data-centre fault can disrupt many firms at once. The outage is an early real-world test of the UK's new regime for supervising those providers and a reminder of why insurers sell cover for cloud failures.

title: APRA Finalises Reinsurance Rule Changes Effective January 1, 2027: Easier Access to Alternative Reinsurance and Fewer Approval Requirements
summary: On July 7, 2026 APRA finalised amendments to its general insurance reinsurance framework, effective January 1, 2027, making alternative reinsurance arrangements easier to access and reducing approval requirements, with updated reporting forms due in the test environment in September 2026.
description:
Australia's prudential regulator has settled new rules for how general insurers manage reinsurance, and they will apply from the start of 2027. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) finalised amendments to its general insurance reinsurance framework on July 7, 2026, according to a summary published by the law firm Regulation Tomorrow. The changes take effect on January 1, 2027. The key standard is GPS 230 Reinsurance Management, the prudential standard that sets out how insurers should manage their reinsurance arrangements.

APRA gave a plain reason for the change: it wants to "ensure that the prudential framework remains fit for purpose as market conditions and reinsurance practices evolve." Reinsurance is insurance purchased by insurers to protect themselves from large losses, such as those from a cyclone or flood. Over recent years, the sources of that protection have diversified. Alongside traditional reinsurers, capital-markets investors now provide cover through instruments such as catastrophe bonds. APRA's earlier changes in this area were reported by the specialist outlet Artemis, which described them as making access to alternative reinsurance easier; those reports concerned the proposals before they were finalised.

The summary lists three kinds of change. First, targeted changes will make alternative reinsurance arrangements easier to access. Second, APRA will reduce the number of approvals it requires, to improve efficiency. Third, there are technical refinements for clarity, consistency and transparency. The summary does not set out the detailed wording, and so it is not possible to say from it exactly which approvals are being dropped or what conditions apply to alternative structures. Readers who need that detail should consult the final standards.

The process was lengthy. APRA consulted twice, in November 2024 and October 2025. After the second round, it adopted the October 2025 proposals with minor clarifications, and published an attachment comparing the two versions. A regulator that adopts its second consultation draft with minor changes is usually signalling that the policy was settled and that the later round tested the drafting rather than the principle, although the sources reviewed do not say that explicitly.

The final package covers a number of instruments. The prudential standards are GPS 115, GPS 116 and GPS 230. The practice guides are GPG 116 and GPG 245. The reporting standards are GRS 115.0, GRS 115.0.G, GRS 115.1, GRS 115.1.G, GRS 116.0 and GRS 116.0.G. Together these set the capital charges and reporting insurers must use when they cede risk to reinsurers, and APRA's guidance on how to meet them.

Implementation is designed to limit workload. Insurers must give APRA a Reinsurance Arrangement Statement (ReAS), a document describing their reinsurance programme. The regulator says insurers do not need to resubmit it solely because of the new framework. Changes will be reflected in their next scheduled ReAS submission. On reporting, APRA said it would release updated forms in the APRA Connect Test environment in September 2026, and planned to publish taxonomy artefacts before then. That timetable should give insurers about three months of testing before the rules take effect.

Why does this matter beyond the industry? Australia is one of the most catastrophe-exposed developed insurance markets, with cyclones in the north, floods along the east coast and bushfires across the south. Reinsurance prices influence what households and businesses pay for property insurance. Globally, reinsurance pricing is expected to fall at the January 2027 renewals, according to analysts, so insurers will be negotiating their programmes at a time when capital is plentiful. Rules that make it simpler to use alternative capital could help insurers take advantage of that supply, but the sources reviewed do not predict any particular price effect, and no such effect should be assumed.

Alternative reinsurance also raises prudential questions that APRA must manage. Collateralised arrangements and capital-markets structures differ from traditional contracts in their counterparty risk, basis risk and legal structure. The summary says only that the changes are targeted and that APRA is retaining controls through the revised standards. It does not describe the safeguards in any detail.

Neighbouring jurisdictions are also developing frameworks. Singapore's regulator, for instance, consulted this year on a protected cell company structure that could host insurance-linked securities, as covered in recent reporting. Such moves suggest regulators across Asia-Pacific are competing to make their markets attractive for alternative risk transfer, while maintaining supervision of risk.

A note on sources and limits. This article relies on a law-firm summary of APRA's announcement and on the structure of the instruments listed there; the full text of the amended standards was not reviewed, and the summary gives no figures for capital charges, thresholds or the number of approvals removed. The January 1, 2027 date is the date from which the amended standards apply, and it coincides with the major reinsurance renewal date, which means insurers will be negotiating programmes for 2027 while finalising their compliance work. Insurers and advisers should therefore read the final GPS 230 and related guides directly before relying on any description of how alternative arrangements will be treated.

For insurers, the immediate tasks are to review their reinsurance programmes against the final standards, prepare to test the updated reporting forms from September, and update their ReAS at the next scheduled submission. For policyholders, the effects will be indirect and slow, if they appear at all. The most direct effect may be a wider choice of risk transfer for the insurers that serve them, and APRA's stated intention is to keep the framework current as the reinsurance market changes.
source_name: Regulation Tomorrow (summary of APRA's July 7, 2026 announcement) and Artemis (earlier reporting on the proposals)
image_alt: Legal and regulatory documents representing prudential standards (illustrative)
key_points: APRA finalised amendments to its general insurance reinsurance framework on July 7, 2026, and the changes take effect on January 1, 2027.

The aim is to keep the prudential framework fit for purpose as market conditions and reinsurance practices evolve, with targeted changes to make alternative reinsurance arrangements easier to access and fewer APRA approvals required.
APRA ran two consultation rounds, in November 2024 and October 2025, and adopted the October 2025 proposals with minor clarifications.
The package covers prudential standards GPS 115, GPS 116 and GPS 230, practice guides GPG 116 and GPG 245, and reporting standards GRS 115 and GRS 116.

Insurers do not need to resubmit their Reinsurance Arrangement Statement solely because of the new framework; changes go into the next scheduled submission, and updated reporting forms will appear in APRA Connect Test in September 2026.
why_it_matters: Australian insurers buy reinsurance to cover cyclone, flood and bushfire losses. Easier use of catastrophe bonds and other non-traditional capital could widen the sources of protection, and fewer approvals reduce paperwork, while APRA keeps control over how insurers rely on their reinsurers.

title: Fitch Says Japan's Big Three Non-Life Insurers Are Well Placed for Strong Underwriting, but Profits Leaned on Selling Strategic Shareholdings
summary: Fitch says Tokio Marine, Sompo and MS&AD improved their combined ratio to 94% in the year to March 2026 from 99%, but combined ordinary profit of ¥2.2 trillion was about 90% disposal gains from strategic shareholdings, which it expects to shrink.
description:
Japan's three largest non-life insurance groups are earning strong underwriting results, but a large part of their headline profit comes from something other than insurance. That is the message of a Fitch Ratings assessment reported by Reinsurance News on June 26, 2026. Although the source is a few months old, it covers the full fiscal year ended March 2026 (which Fitch calls FYE26) and remains the most detailed independent view of the sector's results available at the time of writing; readers should check whether the groups have since published half-year figures.

Fitch says that the three groups, Tokio Marine, Sompo and MS&AD (Mitsui Sumitomo), are "well placed to continue delivering strong underwriting results." It expects underwriting to stay resilient even as investment gains fall. Fitch rates MS&AD A+ with a stable outlook, while Sompo and Tokio Marine are both rated AA- with a stable outlook.

The underwriting improvement is clear in the combined ratio. For the three groups, it improved to 94% in FYE26 from 99% in FYE25. Fitch attributes the better result to stronger underwriting discipline and a better claims environment. A combined ratio of 99% means almost every yen of premium went on claims and costs, while 94% leaves a margin of six yen in every hundred. In domestic motor and property business, Fitch says revised pricing and fewer catastrophe-related claims offset rising vehicle repair costs. Japan is prone to typhoons, floods and earthquakes, so claims from natural catastrophes can swing results sharply; fewer such claims lowered the combined ratio in FYE26.

The profit picture is more complicated. Fitch says that the big three posted combined profits above ¥2 trillion in FYE26, driven mainly by sales of strategic shareholdings. Combined ordinary profit was ¥2.2 trillion, and disposal gains made up 90% of it, compared with 97% the previous year. Strategic shareholdings are the long-standing cross-holdings in client companies that Japanese insurers and banks have held for business relationships. Under pressure from regulators and investors to reduce them, the insurers have been selling the shares, which generates one-off gains. Fitch notes that these gains are excluded from net income under IFRS 17, the international insurance accounting standard, which affects how the profits look to investors.

Fitch expects disposal profits to shrink in FYE27 because the remaining holdings are worth less. This is a key point for the outlook: the sales have given the groups a large one-time boost, but the supply of shares to sell is running down. The insurers will therefore rely more on underwriting and investment income from year to year, which is why Fitch's emphasis on underwriting resilience matters.

Overseas business is a growing pillar. Fitch expects overseas operations to remain a major source of earnings. Growth in US specialty insurance, through both acquisitions and organic expansion, supports underwriting results. Stronger European results boosted MS&AD in particular. The orientation abroad matches the pattern of Japanese life insurers, who are also buying American businesses, as seen in the recent reports about Sumitomo Life and Symetra.

On capital, economic solvency ratios stayed above 200% throughout FYE26. Tokio Marine reported 268% at a 99.5% confidence level, meaning the ratio measures its capital against losses that should be exceeded only once in 200 years. High ratios provide a cushion to absorb losses and fund acquisitions, though the source does not quote ratios for the other two groups.

Accounting is changing. Fitch says the move to IFRS 17 is expected to improve comparability with international peers without materially changing credit profiles. Sompo adopted the standard in FYE26, and MS&AD and Tokio Marine are expected to follow in FYE27. For readers, this means that reported profits for the three groups will not be directly comparable until all have adopted the standard, and that the share-sale gains will no longer appear in net income in the same way.

What should one conclude? First, the underlying business is healthy: a combined ratio of 94% and solvency above 200% indicate substantial strength, and Fitch's ratings are high. Second, headline profit overstates earning power because 90% of ordinary profit came from disposal gains. Third, the cushion will thin as those gains fall, so the groups need to sustain underwriting margins and find new growth, particularly abroad. Fourth, risks remain: rising vehicle repair costs, a bad catastrophe year in Japan, and execution risk on overseas deals could all hurt.

For consumers in Japan, the effects will be mainly in pricing: Fitch says pricing in motor and property has been revised, and further adjustments depend on repair costs and catastrophe experience. For investors and rating watchers, the key indicators to follow are the combined ratio, the share of profit from disposals and the speed of IFRS 17 adoption. The source gives no forecasts for FYE27 profit or combined ratio beyond its general assessment, so no numerical projection is attempted here.

key_points: Fitch says Japan's three largest non-life groups are well placed to keep delivering strong underwriting results even as investment gains fall.
The combined ratio improved to 94% in the fiscal year ended March 2026 (FYE26) from 99% in FYE25, helped by pricing discipline and fewer catastrophe claims.
Combined ordinary profit was ¥2.2 trillion, of which disposal gains from strategic shareholdings made up 90% (97% the year before); Fitch expects these gains to shrink in FYE27.
Fitch rates MS&AD A+/Stable and Sompo and Tokio Marine AA-/Stable, and economic solvency ratios stayed above 200%, with Tokio Marine at 268%.

Overseas operations, especially US specialty insurance and stronger European results, remain a major earnings source, and IFRS 17 adoption continues with MS&AD and Tokio Marine expected to follow Sompo in FYE27.
why_it_matters: Japan's big non-life insurers are among the world's largest and are active buyers of insurers abroad. How much of their profit comes from selling shares rather than from insurance matters for their ability to keep investing overseas and for the stability of one of Asia's biggest insurance markets.
